  • It has been revealed that in response to the rapidly approaching launch of Project Sunrise, Qantas' Airbus A350-1000ULR flights from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Sydney (SYD), Pilot Nick from Lessons from the Flight Deck gave his reflections on what it's like to fly for such extended periods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that SQ23/SQ24, Singapore Airlines' Airbus A350-900ULR flights between Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) and New York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), are a technological and logistical marvel. They cover an average of 9,537 miles (15,348 km), requiring the aircraft to remain in the sky for 18 to 19 hours. The world's longest flight also requires the personnel crewing it to remain sharp throughout.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, such a long flight time well exceeds the legal limits for a two-person flight crew. The flight crew is bolstered to four members, allowing each crew member to use the crew bunk for a four-hour-long and a 2.5-hour-long rest period. These crew members aren't just sticking the A350-900ULR on autopilot and relaxing. It is essential that they are well rested because they have essential duties to carry out while the aircraft is in flight.

It has been revealed that in response to the rapidly approaching launch of Project Sunrise, Qantas' Airbus A350-1000ULR flights from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) to Sydney (SYD), Pilot Nick from Lessons from the Flight Deck gave his reflections on what it's like to fly for such extended periods. He noted that:.

Industry observers note that "The metabolic cost is the constant vigilance. You’re monitoring six fuel tanks, four engine indicators, weather radar, traffic radar, ATC frequencies in three regions, oceanic crossing procedures, alternate airport availability over the next 1,500 miles, and the dozen subtle ways the airplane talks to you.".

The table below is an impression of what pilots will do hour-by-hour on the Singapore to New York flight based on each crew member having a four-hour and a 2.5-hour rest allowance. This is an estimation based on an 18.5-hour flight time. It is clear that ultra-long-haul crew do far more than put the autopilot on and watch the world go by. They also do all of these duties in an environment where the air is thinner, and they are steadily dehydrated.

Recent findings suggest that departure from Singapore. This is a high-workload period, with potential assistance from the reserve crew. It is standard ultra-long-haul procedure to have all four crew members in the cockpit for takeoff and landing.

Recent findings suggest that initial cruising period with regular route, fuel, and weather checks, along with communication with air traffic control. The reserve crew may rest during this period.

Reserve crew returns from rest and takes over for the middle cruise. They'll receive a briefing from the primary crew on anything that they need to be made aware of. The primary captain and first officer may take a rest period.

The first crew returns, allowing the reserve crew to go for their long rest. This is a period of deep cruise, where remote Pacific airspace is crossed.

The reserve crew returns from rest, allowing the primary flight crew to go for their long period of rest. The reserve crew begins to prepare for arrival, with frequent air traffic control communications as they approach and enter US airspace.

The primary crew returns and receives a handover. The approach to New York begins. This is another high-workload period, with the crew having to navigate New York's exceptionally busy airspace before landing and taxiing to the gate.

According to recent reports, one of the main activities that a pilot will be doing aboard Singapore Airlines' flight from Singapore to New York is resting, with each getting almost seven hours away from the flight deck. According to Executive Traveller, A350s come with two upstairs rest areas for pilots and cabin crew members.

The forward rest area, located above the foremost passenger cabin, is for pilots, while the rear rest area is for cabin crew. You can usually tell where these rest areas are because of the lack of central overhead luggage bins. The pilot rest area has two beds, while the cabin crew's space has six bunks. Pilots and crew stay safe in these rest areas because each is concealed behind a steadfast security door with a combination lock.

According to recent reports, these rest areas are concealed behind a sliding screen. Inside is a small staircase that takes the pilot or crew member up to the rest area. In the rest areas, pilots and crew members can sleep, read, or use the WiFi to catch up on their favorite shows. Some airlines also install in-flight entertainment systems. Each bunk is separated by a privacy curtain.

Singapore Airlines' flights from Singapore to New York don't just need pilots who are talented and well-rested. It also requires a plane, which is an undeniable engineering marvel. While the standard A350-900 can fly 8,500 nautical miles (15,742 km), the A350-900ULR, built bespoke for Singapore Airlines, can fly 9,700 nautical miles (17,964 km), with a maximum flight time of 20 hours.

The table below shows specifications for the A350-900ULR according to data from Aircraft Investigation. It shows a high maximum takeoff weight and fuel capacity and a substantially lower passenger capacity than is standard.

2 x Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-84 producing 84,190 lbf (374.5 kN).

Industry observers note that the A350-900ULR will soon no longer be the longest-flying operational A350 variant. That is because of Qantas' Project Sunrise flights from SYD to LHR, which will make use of the upcoming A350-1000ULR. It will be able to fly commercially for up to 22 hours, with test flights exceeding this duration. That will require a reduced seating capacity of just 238 passengers to facilitate a newly introduced 4,400-gallon (20,000-liter) rear-center fuel tank.

Sources indicate that the Project Sunrise philosophy for a better mechanical range is much like the A350-900ULR: more fuel and a higher maximum takeoff weight to sustain it. Airbus engineers have also been hard at work to show that the fuel system can operate safely, particularly in scenarios where large quantities of fuel have to be suddenly diverted.

This aircraft also makes use of the advantages that come as standard with all A350s, such as the 25% fuel efficiency improvement compared with jets of the previous generation. The Rolls-Royce Trent XWB, which exclusively powers this aircraft family, is also known for being among the world's most efficient widebody engines. The jet achieves all of this while having a 50% lower noise footprint than the A330.

It has been revealed that as with Singapore Airlines' ultra-long-haul A350 flights, Project Sunrise trips will be crewed by four pilots, with long and short rest periods built into the schedule. All four pilots will usually make their way to the flight deck during the busiest periods, such as takeoff and landing. These systems have been standardized by ultra-long-haul carriers such as Singapore Airlines, Qantas, Emirates, and Cathay Pacific over the past 20 years.

Project Sunrise flights will cross between nine and eleven time zones, depending on the exact time of year that they will be flying. Qantas' circadian rhythm research will help pilots to recover more rapidly from jet lag. Meal times, lighting, and rest cycles will need to be carefully choreographed with this need in mind.

Anticipation is growing for Project Sunrise, which is set to launch in 2027.

It isn't just the flight from Singapore to Latest York that is long enough for pilots to need plenty of rest. After all, Singapore Airlines also has plenty of other long routes that originate at Singapore Changi Airport (SIN). Away from New York, the North American destinations are Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) on the West Coast.

According to recent reports, singapore Airlines also flies its A350-900ULRs to five European airports. These are Manchester Airport (MAN), London Heathrow Airport (LHR), London Gatwick Airport (LGW), Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD), and Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat Airport (BCN). The final destination is Cape Town International (CPT).

It has been revealed that the shortest of these routes is the 14-hour-and-ten-minute flight to Cape Town, which is operated via Johannesburg (JNB). This route is operated daily. The most frequent route is to San Francisco, which operates twice daily. The flights to LGW are less regular but peak at twice daily. Finally, the longest routes are to the two Fresh York airports, both of which have a block time exceeding 19 hours.

Sources indicate that the A350-900ULR deviates from Singapore Airlines' standard A350 layout of 253 seats across three classes. This features 42 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, 24 premium economy seats in a 2-4-2 layout, and 187 economy seats in a 3-3-3 configuration.

Singapore Airlines' A350-900ULR configuration has space for just 161 passengers, with 67 business class seats and room for 94 premium economy passengers. Meanwhile, there is no economy cabin, and the jets will soon be reconfigured with an even more exclusive 132-seat layout.

#195. Tech Report: Why Boeing 787 Cockpits Use Electronic Checklists Instead Of Paper

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Tech Report: Why Boeing 787 Cockpits Use Electronic Checklists Instead Of Paper

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door.
  • Industry observers note that the Boeing 787 Dreamliner's flight deck is designed around digital information.
  • In a recent development, this is more than a change in presentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

Industry observers note that the Boeing 787 Dreamliner's flight deck is designed around digital information. Large displays bring together flight data, navigation information, aircraft system indications, and alerts, giving pilots access to information that once appeared across numerous separate instruments and documents. The aircraft’s electronic checklist system follows the same philosophy. Instead of relying solely on printed pages, pilots can access normal and non-normal checklists through the flight deck displays.

In a recent development, this is more than a change in presentation. An electronic checklist can connect checklist procedures with aircraft alerts and, where the system supports it, use aircraft signals to confirm that certain actions have been completed. That can help pilots keep track of a procedure, avoid overlooking steps after an interruption, and manage abnormal situations more systematically. Paper checklists still have an notable role, however. Understanding why Boeing adopted electronic checklists means looking at how they work, what they improve, and where their limitations remain.

Sources indicate that the 787’s electronic checklist system is integrated into the aircraft’s flight deck information environment. It provides access to normal checklists, which cover routine phases of flight, and non-normal checklists, which address situations requiring a specific response. Rather than searching through a paper manual, pilots can select the relevant procedure on a display and work through its instructions in sequence.

Sources indicate that the relationship between the checklist system and the aircraft alerting system is particularly important during non-normal operations. When the aircraft detects a condition that generates an applicable alert, the flight crew can access the associated checklist through the flight deck controls. On the 787, selecting the checklist function can bring up the relevant procedure on a multifunction display. If several alerts have associated checklists, the system can present them for the crew to select. This gives pilots a more direct route from an aircraft indication to the procedure intended to address it.

Industry observers note that electronic checklists can also provide information about whether individual actions have been completed. Some items are designed as closed-loop steps, meaning the system receives a signal from the aircraft that can confirm the required configuration or action. Other items are open-loop steps, which require the pilot to verify completion manually. The distinction matters because an electronic checklist does not automatically know whether every action has been performed simply because a pilot has selected or acknowledged an item.

A closer look at some of the most cutting-edge aircraft in 2026.

Paper checklists are straightforward, familiar, and independent of an aircraft's display systems. They have served flight crews for decades, but they also create practical challenges in a modern cockpit. A pilot must locate the correct page, maintain their place while reading, and ensure that the checklist continues from the correct point after an interruption. During a busy phase of flight, even a small loss of place can require the crew to retrace steps and confirm which actions have already been completed.

In a recent development, an electronic checklist addresses several of these difficulties by keeping the procedure within the flight deck display environment. The crew can access the required checklist without handling a separate document, while the system can provide visual indications of progress. Where aircraft data supports automatic confirmation, the display can also distinguish between an action that has been verified by the system and one that still requires a pilot's confirmation. This reduces some of the administrative work involved in tracking a checklist, although it does not remove the need for careful monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that the move toward electronic checklists also reflects the wider development of flight deck automation. As aircraft systems became more integrated, manufacturers had opportunities to connect operating procedures with alerts and aircraft configuration information. Boeing's work on electronic checklists predates the 787. The manufacturer's development of the technology began decades earlier, with its system evolving through the 1990s and becoming part of the Boeing 777 flight deck. The 787 builds on that broader move toward integrated flight deck information rather than representing the beginning of electronic checklist technology.

One of the most key features of an electronic checklist is the difference between closed-loop and open-loop items. Although both appear within the same procedure, they do not work in the same way. A closed-loop item can receive confirmation from an aircraft system or sensor, while an open-loop item depends on the flight crew to perform and verify the action. Understanding this distinction helps explain why an electronic checklist is more than a digital version of a printed page.

For a closed-loop item, the checklist system can use information from the aircraft to determine whether the required condition has been achieved. For example, if a checklist step requires a particular switch or system configuration, an appropriate aircraft signal may allow the system to recognize that the condition has been met. The checklist indication can then change to show completion. The exact indications and available feedback depend on the aircraft system and the individual checklist item.

Can receive confirmation from aircraft data or a system signal.

Can enhancement when the required condition is detected.

Pilot still monitors the action and system response.

Only works where suitable aircraft feedback is available.

An open-loop item works differently. The system cannot independently confirm that the required action has been carried out, so the pilot must complete the task and verify it. This is crucial for actions that depend on human observation, judgment, or confirmation rather than a signal available to the checklist computer. Electronic presentation does not turn every checklist instruction into an automatically verified action. The crew remains responsible for ensuring that each step has been completed correctly.

The aircraft offers exceptional long-haul capabilities.

Electronic checklists are particularly useful when an aircraft generates a non-normal alert. In these circumstances, pilots may need to identify the condition, locate the applicable procedure, assess the aircraft's status, and carry out a series of actions. The checklist system helps connect the alert with the relevant procedure, reducing the need to search manually through a collection of printed pages while managing other flight deck tasks.

It has been revealed that on the Boeing 787, the electronic checklist system works alongside the aircraft's alerting functions. When an alert has an associated checklist, pilots can use the checklist control to access the procedure on a multifunction display. If more than one alert requires a checklist, the crew can be presented with the available procedures and select the one they need. The system therefore helps organize procedural information, but it does not make operational decisions on behalf of the pilots.

Sources indicate that the display also helps crews monitor progress through a procedure. This is particularly relevant when a checklist is interrupted or when several tasks must be managed at the same time. A clear indication of checklist status can help pilots establish which items have been completed and which remain outstanding. Nevertheless, the crew must continue to monitor the aircraft, communicate effectively, and apply the procedure in the context of the situation. The checklist is a tool for supporting those responsibilities, not a substitute for them.

It has been revealed that electronic checklists offer clear advantages, but they also depend on the availability and correct operation of the aircraft's electronic systems. A display failure, checklist system fault, or loss of relevant system feedback can affect how the crew accesses or completes a procedure. For that reason, paper checklists and approved alternative procedures remain notable parts of the wider operational framework. The presence of an electronic checklist does not mean printed procedures are unnecessary.

The Boeing 787's minimum equipment procedures recognize that the electronic checklist system can be unavailable under specified conditions. If the system is inoperative, the applicable maintenance and operational provisions require it to be deactivated and suitable checklist procedures to be used. There are also provisions for situations in which closed-loop indications are unavailable. In those circumstances, crews may need to use the prescribed line-item override procedures to complete the checklist. These provisions demonstrate that the aircraft has procedures for dealing with checklist system limitations rather than assuming the electronic system will always be available.

Available independently of the checklist display.

Require the crew to locate the relevant procedure.

Can confirm supported aircraft configurations.

Depend on functioning electronic equipment.

Provide an alternative when approved procedures require their use.

Paper procedures also provide another way to access information. They do not rely on the checklist display itself, and they can serve as a practical backup when the approved procedures call for their use. However, paper is not automatically safer or more reliable in every situation. A printed checklist can be misplaced, difficult to manage during a busy phase of flight, or harder to track after an interruption. The key point is that electronic and paper procedures have different strengths, and the aircraft's approved operating documentation determines which method to use in a given circumstance.

Sources indicate that explore the striking Airbus A320 vs. Boeing 737 cockpit differences, from sidesticks to noise, and learn how pilots see these iconic flight decks.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage of an electronic checklist is not simply that it removes paper from the cockpit. Its value comes from how it organizes information and, where the aircraft supports it, connects procedures with aircraft system data. A pilot can access an applicable checklist through the flight deck interface, follow its sequence, and receive confirmation for certain actions. That integration can make checklist management more consistent and help reduce errors associated with losing place or overlooking a step after an interruption.

However, electronic systems introduce their own considerations. Pilots must understand how the checklist interface works, recognize the difference between automatically confirmed and manually verified items, and avoid treating a completed indication as proof that the entire aircraft is in the correct condition. A system can only confirm what its sensors and programmed logic are designed to monitor. It cannot replace the crew's responsibility to assess the aircraft, recognize unexpected conditions and apply sound judgment.

The Boeing 787's electronic checklist system therefore represents an evolution in how flight crews manage procedures, rather than an attempt to remove human involvement. It brings checklists closer to the aircraft information they depend on, provides a structured way to monitor progress and supports access to non-normal procedures when alerts occur. Paper procedures remain part of the operational backup framework, while pilots retain responsibility for every action and verification. The technology has changed how the checklist is presented, but the essential purpose remains the same: ensuring that critical actions are completed, checked, and understood before the flight moves on.

Recent findings suggest that journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Sources indicate that travel chaos may continue to linger across the US tonight and into tomorrow, after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the rare nationwide ground stop across airports nationwide. This comes as thousands of airline crew and aircraft remain displaced.

In a recent development, on Friday, a ground stop forced all aircraft to be grounded for more than four hours due to a telecommunications and tech outage stemming from overloaded routers and data inconsistencies. With the Department of Homeland Security explaining that this came from the patching of a new system into the existing framework that led to the older system to become overwhelmed.

Passengers are encouraged to be patient and reconfirm the status of their flights before heading to the airport. President and Chief Executive Officer of Airlines for America, Chris Sununu, spoke with NewsNation and reiterated that while the agency moved quickly to glitch the nationwide ground stop for safety concerns until affected systems were restored, this has displaced thousands of airline crew members and many aircraft nationwide.

It is expected that the side effects of the ground stop could be felt by passengers for days, as airlines work around the clock to deal with affected aircraft, crew and passengers. According to CNN, it is suggested that more than 7,500 flights within, into, or out of the US were canceled today following the ground stop.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to canceled flights, more than 10,000 flights experienced delays. The knock-on effect is already hampering Saturday's flight plans, with more than 1,500 flights already being canceled.

The ground stop has sent ripples out across the globe, with many flights destined for the US delayed. While airspace was reopened at 8:15 PM on Friday, flight departures would only resume gradually, and it will take time for airlines to be able to fully restore operations. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted, 'it's going to be slow'.

Industry observers note that highlighted from this event is the ongoing strain of the US air traffic control system, which is plagued with aging technology, equipment and communication problems. This pressure is amplified by the severe shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers. However, in the face of today's travel chaos, some air traffic controllers have already expressed that they 'don't buy' Duffy's explanation for what happened, with Anna Giaritelli telling CNN that a main reason is:.

“These types of switches they’re doing that the FAA is doing, they don’t happen during the day. They don’t happen during busy times like a Friday afternoon. They’re doing these midweek, in the middle of the night when there is no air traffic going on.”.

In a recent development, trouble first was identified at 3:36 PM, when air traffic control centres across the country noted instability in radar and communication systems. This quickly escalated with switches and routers that carry critical data becoming overloaded. As a result, inconsistent information from these systems prompted the FAA to issue the rare ground stop for flights nationwide.

The agency cited communication problems for the halt.

A ground stop is exactly what it sounds like, restricting flight operations on the ground. This meant that aircraft already in the air were permitted to continue to their intended destinations without major disruption. Thousands of aircraft were able to land safely during the ground stop; however, no jets were permitted to depart.

According to recent reports, homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed that the FAA updates to the aging systems were the reason behind the ground stop, and the halt in flight operations was not due to a threat to the US, and had no links to the Thursday Microsoft outage. The Transportation Secretary has also warned that there could be more disruption in the future unless systems are updated.

Industry observers note that as airlines resume flight operations, displaced crew, passengers and aircraft will slowly return to normal; however, this is expected to take several days until services are back to normal. It is not expected to impact the upcoming Thanksgiving travel rush in late November.

#193. Latest Update: Here's What Passengers Actually Get For The Extra Fare Of Premium Economy & Why It's Increasingly Popular

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9 min read (1742 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Latest Update: Here's What Passengers Actually Get For The Extra Fare Of Premium Economy & Why It's Increasingly Popular

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, premium economy has become an increasingly popular option for passengers on long-haul flights, offering significantly more comfort than economy class without the considerably higher fares associated with business class.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to Going's 2026 State of Travel report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among surveyed travelers, increasing from 16% to 20% in just one year.
  • The most noticeable difference between premium economy and regular economy class is the amount of personal space available to passengers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, premium economy has become an increasingly popular option for passengers on long-haul flights, offering significantly more comfort than economy class without the considerably higher fares associated with business class. In recent years, the cabin has become an important part of the long-haul products of carriers such as Delta Air Lines, Lufthansa, Emirates, and British Airways. Airlines are also continuing to increase the number of seats on their aircraft, often at the expense of regular economy capacity.

Recent findings suggest that according to Going's 2026 State of Travel report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among surveyed travelers, increasing from 16% to 20% in just one year. This growing popularity comes as airlines invest heavily in premium products, while passengers become more willing to pay extra for comfort. However, with premium economy fares generally costing 30% to 100% more than regular economy, what do passengers actually get for the extra money?

The most noticeable difference between premium economy and regular economy class is the amount of personal space available to passengers. On most long-haul aircraft, economy class seats have a pitch of approximately 30 to 32 inches (76 to 81 cm), compared to around 38 to 40 inches (97 to 102 cm) in premium economy. Seat pitch is the distance between the same point on two consecutive rows of seats, meaning passengers generally get around seven to nine additional inches of space between seats.

Premium economy seats are also considerably wider than those found in economy class. While regular economy seats typically measure between 17 and 18 inches (43 to 46 cm), premium economy seats are often between 18.5 and 19.5 inches (47 to 50 cm) wide. Most airlines also provide additional recline, generally between six and eight inches (15 to 20 cm), and many seats feature adjustable headrests, calf rests, and footrests. These differences become particularly noticeable on overnight flights, where passengers may spend eight to 12 hours in the same seat.

However, the actual differences depend on the airline and aircraft type. Lufthansa's new Allegris premium economy product, for example, offers 39 inches (99 cm) of seat pitch and features a fixed-shell design that lets passengers recline without disturbing the person behind them. Other carriers, including Emirates and Cathay Pacific, offer premium economy seats with up to 40 inches of pitch, while certain airlines provide even more space.

It seems to be one of the use of space aboard aircraft for maximizing revenue.

Besides the extra space, most airlines include other benefits for passengers traveling in premium economy. On long-haul flights, this often includes upgraded meal services, a wider selection of drinks, and better-quality amenities than those provided in regular economy. Depending on the airline, passengers may receive a welcome drink before departure, meals served on proper tableware, noise-canceling headphones, and an amenity kit. Many airlines have also installed larger inflight entertainment screens and additional power outlets in their premium economy seats.

Emirates, for example, provides its premium economy passengers with upgraded dining, including meals served on proper tableware, along with larger entertainment screens and more personal space. Lufthansa has also improved its premium economy offering through its Allegris product, introducing wireless charging, additional storage compartments, and privacy features. These investments are part of a broader effort to differentiate premium economy from regular economy rather than simply selling passengers a seat with additional legroom.

The differences also extend to the airport experience, as many airlines provide priority check-in and boarding. Moreover, premium economy fares often include a larger checked baggage allowance than economy tickets. However, these benefits can vary considerably depending on the airline and fare type, and lounge access is generally not included. For example, some airlines offer lower-priced premium economy fares with reduced baggage allowances, so passengers should not assume every premium economy ticket includes the same benefits.

Sources indicate that it is also crucial to distinguish premium economy from extra-legroom economy products, such as United Airlines' Economy Plus. While these seats generally provide more legroom, passengers still receive the same basic seat and onboard service as regular economy travelers. Dedicated premium economy cabins, such as United Premium Plus or Delta Premium Select, offer wider seats and a different onboard product. However, unlike modern business class suites, these seats do not convert into fully flat beds.

It seems to be one of the use of space aboard aircraft for maximizing revenue.

Premium economy is generally considerably more expensive than a regular economy class ticket, with passengers often paying between 30% and 100% more for the additional comfort and services. However, the actual difference depends heavily on the airline, route, and time of booking. While the upgrade can sometimes be relatively affordable, particularly on longer flights, premium economy fares can also approach those of discounted business class tickets.

In a recent development, to put these differences into perspective, Simple Flying previously compared British Airways' premium economy and business class fares on three of the airline's busiest transatlantic routes from London Heathrow Airport (LHR). The analysis, conducted on May 25, 2026, examined one-way fares to New York, Boston, and Los Angeles for travel during July 2026 and February 2027.

Industry observers note that london - John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

London - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS).

London - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

It has been revealed that during the peak summer travel period, premium economy fares averaged €3,181 ($3,516) across the three routes, compared with €9,587 ($10,596) for business class. This represented a saving of approximately €6,400 ($7,080), or nearly 67%, for passengers choosing World Traveller Plus instead of Club World. Nevertheless, even premium economy tickets were far from inexpensive, with one-way fares exceeding €3,500 ($3,868) on the route to Los Angeles.

John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

London - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Sources indicate that for travel in February 2027, the average premium economy fare was significantly lower at €1,337 ($1,478), compared with €2,085 ($2,304) for business class. However, the difference between the two cabins also narrowed substantially, with passengers saving an average of €748 ($827).

In a recent development, importantly, the February flights were examined approximately nine months before departure, while the July flights were only one to two months away. Consequently, the large differences between summer and winter fares cannot be attributed to seasonality alone, as booking lead times and available fare classes also influence prices, but they still provide a rough indication.

USD equivalents have been converted using the European Central Bank's reference exchange rate of €1 = $1.1052 on November 13, 2026. The original fares were collected on May 25, 2026, and do not represent current ticket prices.

The differences go far beyond price, with business class passengers enjoying more space, better service, and lounge access.

Sources indicate that according to Going's 2026 State of Travel and Flight Deals report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among the travelers surveyed, increasing from 16% to 20% over the previous year. Furthermore, 59% of respondents indicated that they intended to spend more on premium cabin seating during 2026, making it one of the most popular travel upgrades. The same report found that 71% of travelers planned to spend more on accommodation, suggesting that many passengers are increasingly willing to spend more on the quality of their trips rather than simply taking additional vacations.

Part of the increasing demand for premium economy also comes from business travelers, particularly as companies are looking for ways to control their travel expenses. While business class remains an notable product for corporate travel, some employers are reconsidering whether employees need fully lie-flat seats on every long-haul journey.

According to recent reports, at the same time, affluent leisure travelers have become an increasingly crucial customer group for premium cabins after the pandemic. Unlike corporate travelers, these passengers generally pay for their own tickets and may be willing to spend additional money on comfort, particularly when traveling for longer vacations or special occasions. This has also blurred the traditional distinction between premium cabins designed primarily for corporate passengers and economy cabins serving leisure travelers.

These seats are often exceptionally comfortable.

While passengers benefit from additional comfort, premium economy has also become an notable revenue-generating product for airlines. This is partly because premium economy seats occupy considerably less space than business class seats, while still allowing airlines to charge significantly more than regular economy fares.

Unlike business class, which requires considerably more space for lie-flat beds and privacy features, premium economy generally uses seats that are only somewhat larger than those in economy. Airlines can therefore charge higher fares without necessarily sacrificing as much seating capacity. Of course, generating more revenue per square foot does not automatically mean that premium economy is more profitable, as this also depends on the costs of providing the additional services and the fares passengers are willing to pay.

In a recent development, the broader shift toward premium travel has also become increasingly visible in airline financial results. During the second quarter of 2026, Delta Air Lines reported $6.92 billion in premium passenger revenue, compared to $6.85 billion in Main Cabin revenue. This marked the first time the airline's premium ticket revenue exceeded its Main Cabin revenue, although the figures include all premium products rather than premium economy alone. In the third quarter, Delta generated another $6.82 billion in premium revenue, up 18% from the previous year, while premium seating capacity increased by 6%.

It has been revealed that with passenger demand for premium economy continuing to grow, airlines are allocating an increasing proportion of their long-haul aircraft cabins to premium economy. Airlines such as American Airlines, Emirates, and Alaska Airlines are all continuing to invest heavily in their premium economy cabins. Cathay Pacific, for example, increased its premium economy capacity on updated Boeing 777-300ER aircraft from 34 to 48 seats, representing an increase of approximately 41%. Air France also doubled the size of its premium economy cabin from 24 to 48 seats on certain retrofitted 777-300ERs. These changes demonstrate how airlines are adjusting existing aircraft configurations rather than relying exclusively on new aircraft deliveries to expand their premium offerings.

#191. The US Quietly Raided Switzerland's F-35 Account To Pay For Patriot Missiles — Here's What Happened Next

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

The US Quietly Raided Switzerland's F-35 Account To Pay For Patriot Missiles — Here's What Happened Next

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The crunch on America's strategic missile stockpile put Switzerland in a tough position in 2025 when the United States informed Swiss leaders that it would be pausing Raytheon Patriot missile deliveries.
  • In a recent development, the Swiss government halted payments under its foreign military sales contract that funds the Patriot program; however, the US simply withdrew the outstanding balance from cash earmarked for Swiss fighters.
  • In a recent development, switzerland is in the process of transitioning its fleet from the Boeing F/A-18 Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The crunch on America's strategic missile stockpile put Switzerland in a tough position in 2025 when the United States informed Swiss leaders that it would be pausing Raytheon Patriot missile deliveries. Washington declared that the supply chain diversion was necessary to prioritize shipments to Ukraine and replenish the domestic arsenal.

In a recent development, the Swiss government halted payments under its foreign military sales contract that funds the Patriot program; however, the US simply withdrew the outstanding balance from cash earmarked for Swiss fighters. Instead of creating a leverage point in negotiations to resume Patriot deliveries, the Swiss aircraft supply chain was now in jeopardy.

In a recent development, switzerland is in the process of transitioning its fleet from the Boeing F/A-18 Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II. Switzerland had paid up front in 2021 to secure its position on the production line, but amid the missile dispute, the US now demanded additional payments. American officials not only demanded that the Swiss repay the funds withdrawn for Patriot missiles.

Rather, they also increased the total based on rising production costs, inflation, and supply chain pressures. The US now claims that the contract's original fixed price could not be enforced and is demanding an additional $760 million to $1.5 billion. Instead of paying higher fees, Switzerland cut its order book by 20%, dropping from 36 Joint Strike Fighters to 30.

Industry observers note that under the terms and conditions of the FMS agreements between the US and Switzerland, Washington had the authority to take funding from any pool of Swiss defense program funds. Because the contract allows the US to shift resources if one project runs short on cash, Washington legally bypassed the freeze. It redirected well over 100 million Swiss francs, or $126 million.

Sources indicate that since these events, Swiss lawmakers have openly debated the reliability of Washington as a security partner and considered European alternatives for future defense needs. The Swiss government was bound by a strict, voter-approved budget ceiling, and doubts were beginning to arise concerning the quality of the F-35 as well as the level of control that the US held over the jets after delivery.

The combined friction of the FMS fund redirection, delivery delays, and soaring jet costs has strained US-Swiss defense relations. Urs Loher, head of the Swiss Armaments Agency Armasuisse, described the situation as "very unsatisfactory," according to Blue News. Loher was quoted by Swiss Info as saying that "the risk was too great for us. We'll take whatever we can get.".

Recent findings suggest that to avoid risking the delivery of the F-35s or spare parts for their existing F/A-18 fleet, the Swiss Defense Ministry had to quietly transfer tens of millions in advance to plug the resulting budget hole. The financial strain of the FMS pricing dispute forced the Swiss government to fundamentally restructure its Air2030 modernization prepares. Adding to Swiss frustration, a US Government Accountability Office report confirmed that the early Swiss aircraft will be delivered in a truncated Block 4 software configuration.

Industry observers note that the F-35 program and US-Swiss defense relations have significantly deteriorated, evolving from a strict procurement disagreement into an ongoing diplomatic crisis. Over the first half of 2026, the dispute reached a critical tipping point, resulting in official order reductions, massive advanced Swiss outlays, and public threats from Bern to terminate parts of its defense contracts.

Sources indicate that in April, Swiss Defense Minister Martin Pfister announced that Switzerland is actively negotiating a potential termination of the entire Patriot missile contract. Despite the political gridlock, the physical program has forged ahead out of sheer contractual necessity. The first Swiss F-35A entered main assembly at Lockheed Martin’s Marietta, Georgia, plant.

Sources indicate that full Block 4 modernization will not be ready until 2031 at the earliest, creating a massive capability gap as older Swiss fleets age. The initial batch of aircraft will be deployed to Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas for pilot training, with physical arrivals in Switzerland delayed until 2028. Despite cutting aircraft, the programmatic costs continue to swell. In June 2026, the Swiss Council of States approved an additional credit of $505 million.

Swiss pilots will begin training on the first eight aircraft at Ebbing starting in mid-2027. Following the delivery of the first platform, the remaining airframes are slated to undergo final assembly and checkout at the European production line in Cameri, Italy. Because the timelines have become so volatile, the Swiss government has had to scramble to extend the life of its aging fleet of Hornets.

Warsaw's search for the next air superiority platform.

Switzerland's F/A-18 Hornet Service Life Extension Program has become an expensive, high-stakes anchor for air defense following changes to the F-35 procurement. To free up emergency cash internally and protect the baseline F-35 purchase, Switzerland had to scale back the depth of its Hornet upgrades.

Recent findings suggest that while 30 planes were initially included in the full scope of retrofits, 15 will receive more limited upgrades to save costs. The structural refurbishments were completed across all 30 aircraft. Still, with ongoing uncertainty over the F-35 delivery dates, Switzerland will also study the extreme measure of stretching the F/A-18 fleet beyond 2030 and past the 6,000-hour structural safety limit.

They are also expecting to continue flying the decades-old Northrop F-5 Tigers until the end of 2030. The Swiss Air Force flies high-G, tight-turning air-policing missions through narrow alpine valleys, making structural work non-negotiable.

Industry observers note that the concern is that only 15 of the 30 Swiss Hornets received the intended radar updates, modern flight-management software, and secure communications overhauls. This created a split fleet. Half of the Swiss Hornets possess airframes certified to fly structurally into the 2030s but carry outdated radar and electronic warfare systems, leaving them highly vulnerable if deployed in modern battle space.

The chronic problems keeping the fleet of stealth fighters grounded.

The Swiss Federal Council officially stated that any future purchases to bring the fleet back up to its originally required 36 aircraft will be evaluated independently of aircraft type. Instead of buying more JSFs, Switzerland is considering a mixed fleet by pairing the 30 F-35s with 4.5-generation European-made aircraft. Drones could provide a low-cost means of filling the capability gap alongside F-35s.

It has been revealed that in terms of crewed platforms, the top contenders are the Eurofighter, Rafale, and Gripen. Airbus previously offered Switzerland a robust industrial package to accompany an order for the Eurofighter Typhoon. The Typhoon excels at high-altitude, high-speed interception, which fits the Swiss alpine air-policing mandate perfectly. Pairing it with the F-35 would reduce Swiss reliance on a single US supply chain.

Recent findings suggest that dassault's Rafale was a top contender in the original evaluation that led to the F-35 selection as successor to the Hornet. Because Switzerland shares a border and close diplomatic ties with France, choosing the Rafale for a second batch would simplify training and logistics.

Dassault makes both a land-based and carrier-capable variant, and the Rafale F4 is built as the ultimate omnirole fighter jet capable of exceptional air-to-air and air-to-ground performance. Though Saab pulled out of the original flight tests because the Gripen E wasn't fully operational at the time, it remains the ultimate 'budget-friendly' 4.5-generation option.

It has been revealed that its operating cost per flight hour is a fraction of the F-35's, making it an ideal candidate for basic peacetime air policing. The Royal Canadian Air Force has also been considering the Gripen E as an alternative, while Canada is still struggling to decide whether it will fulfill its original order for 88 F-35s due to diplomatic disputes between Ottawa and Washington, as Bern experienced.

Fifth-generation fighters still struggling to live up to the hype.

Industry observers note that the ultimate alternative would be to follow suit with some other European Air Forces that have decided to skip fifth-generation fighter technology altogether and go straight to sixth-generation stealth jets. Although the trilateral Future Combat Air System program fell through between Germany, France, and Spain, there is an alternative.

In a recent development, the Global Combat Air Program is progressing in partnership with the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan. Germany is considering joining the FCAS, relegated to a combat cloud and advanced drone development program. The aircraft is expected to be on par with the Next Generation Air Dominance aircraft, or the Boeing F-47.

It has been revealed that canada and even India are also considering joining the GCAP program at various levels of investment. The primary roadblock to Switzerland joining the multinational program is likely the price point. The GCAP, also known as the BAE Tempest, could be as expensive as $300 million if it were to cost a similar amount to its American equivalent.

In a recent development, the price of an F-35A is around $90 million for the US Air Force, but that doesn't include the add-on cost for support that FMS customers pay, which can increase the flyaway cost by as much as 50%. That would still be half or less of a GCAP, assuming it is priced comparably to the F-47. That may not be realistic for Bern.

However, if they are only planning to procure a half dozen jets on a case-by-case basis, then the value of a small 'exquisite' sub-fleet with European support would significantly elevate Swiss air power. Still, the capabilities of a collaborative combat aircraft, also known as a loyal wingman drone, are likely a better fit if the Swiss Air Force chooses an advanced platform rather than a 4.5-Gen fighter jet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quark Expeditions has announced that it once again reached the emperor penguin colony at Snow Hill, allowing 137 guests to stand among more than 4,000 breeding pairs and their chicks.

The landing, led by Expedition Leader Ryan McDevitt, came one day after Quark marked 22 years since a team under former Expedition Leader Susan Adie made polar history as the first operator to bring guests to the remote rookery.

In a recent development, julie Chen, a guest from Sacramento, California, mentioned: “As soon as [we arrived at Snow Hill], I was just so excited. There were so many [Emperor penguins]. And they are just beautiful, beautiful, beautiful little penguins. And they all have these little personalities when you start looking at each one of them. It’s almost indescribable.”.

Located on the sea ice off the south coast of Snow Hill Island in Antarctica’s Weddell Sea, the emperor penguin colony is one of the most challenging locations on the continent to reach, the company mentioned in a press release.

Over the course of two days, guests on “Emperor Penguin Quest: Expedition to Snow Hill” departed the Ultramarine in small groups aboard its two twin-engine helicopters.

Flying over the vast expanse of the Weddell Sea and past immense tabular icebergs, guests landed on the sea ice before making the final approach on foot to the emperor penguin colony.

Behind the experience was an operation led by Expedition Leader Ryan McDevitt alongside a polar-specialized Ultramarine team including Captain Roy Laud, Lead Pilot Jonathan Mutch, and Head Mountain Guide Phil Wickens.

It has been revealed that “It’s a huge operation, logistically challenging, and to do it safely is gratifying, remarked McDevitt. “[I’m] just super proud of the whole crew of Ultramarine for making it all happen.”.

#187. Watch: 3 Rock Bands Play Mid-Air Concert On Southwest Jet That Narrowly Beat FAA Ground Stop

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words)
Gadgets 🌐 Simpleflying

Watch: 3 Rock Bands Play Mid-Air Concert On Southwest Jet That Narrowly Beat FAA Ground Stop

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Passengers on a Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Orlando on Friday got an unexpected in-flight concert from three of the biggest rock bands of the early 2000s.
  • The flight departed from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) just moments before the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) unveiled a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, bringing all US departures to a halt for more than four hours.
  • In a recent development, videos from the flight show the cabin lights dimmed as passengers sang along, raised their arms and filmed the performances on their phones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Passengers on a Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Orlando on Friday got an unexpected in-flight concert from three of the biggest rock bands of the early 2000s. Hoobastank, Simple Blueprint and The Used each took turns performing in the aisle, with videos shared by passengers later spreading across social media.

The flight departed from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) just moments before the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) unveiled a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, bringing all US departures to a halt for more than four hours. According to some onboard, the Southwest flight was among the last to take off before the order took effect.

In a recent development, videos from the flight show the cabin lights dimmed as passengers sang along, raised their arms and filmed the performances on their phones. According to the Daily Voice, Hoobastank frontman Doug Robb performed the band's 2004 hit "The Reason," while Simple Plan followed with "Perfect" and "I'm Just a Kid," and The Used played "The Taste of Ink.".

All three bands are scheduled to appear at this weekend's Vans Warped Tour event in Orlando, of which Southwest is an event sponsor. Hoobastank later shared several passenger videos to its Instagram Stories, including one from singer LØLØ, who captioned her clip, "Every plane was grounded today, but the emo gods made sure this one flew.".

Recent findings suggest that it is not clear whether the performances had been planned or were spontaneous. Southwest is listed as the Preferred Airline Partner of Vans Warped Tour. The festival's website says the airline is bringing "the first-ever Vans Warped Tour experience at 35,000 feet" through its Live at 35 program, which features pop-up performances on flights.

Simple Flying contacted Southwest for comment about this flight, but a representative could not be reached before publication.

Southwest introduced its Live at 35 program in 2011, bringing musicians onboard to perform for passengers. The program held its 100th concert in October 2024, when Liz Rose performed on a flight from Nashville to Miami. The flight was carrying Taylor Swift fans to the Eras Tour.

In June, the carrier marked 15 years of the initiative with a performance by the Plain White T's, one of the program's earliest acts. The airline mentioned at the time that it planned to hold more of these onboard events in the coming months, and several have since taken place.

Other notable performances include Bowling For Soup performing on a flight to Las Vegas in July, while reggae artist Julian Marley recently performed on a sold-out flight from Orlando to Montego Bay. The onboard performances are typically brief, with a Southwest spokesperson previously stating that each lasts about 10 minutes.

Stranded crews and grounded jets paint chaotic airport scenes as tech failures ripple through nationwide schedules.

The Southwest flight's departure came just before one of the most significant disruptions to US air travel in decades. At 3:54 PM ET (12:54 PM local time in Los Angeles), the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop, later describing the glitch as a "temporary telecommunications outage.".

Sources indicate that while aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations, all departing flights were held on the ground until the restriction was lifted at around 8:15 PM ET. At over four hours, it was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years and only the second since the September 11 attacks, following a January 2023 malfunction of the FAA system used to send notices to pilots.

It has been revealed that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said aging air traffic control routers had become overloaded with data, while other officials claimed that latest technology being installed had overwhelmed older equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed there was no indication of a cyberattack or terrorist threat.

#185. Here's How Boeing Killed 2 Birds With 1 Stone When It Built The 767's Gear Unlike Any Other Jet

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1535 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Here's How Boeing Killed 2 Birds With 1 Stone When It Built The 767's Gear Unlike Any Other Jet

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Boeing 767 is unique among Boeing aircraft for its main landing gear sporting a 'toe-down' (or forward tilting) position.
  • The toe-down position is one of the easiest ways to visually identify a landing Boeing 767 from other Boeing widebodies, although not so much from Airbus aircraft, as some models have a similar configuration.
  • In a recent development, the Boeing 767 has an unusual feature noted in the aviation community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Boeing 767 is unique among Boeing aircraft for its main landing gear sporting a 'toe-down' (or forward tilting) position. The front wheels make contact with the runway before the rear wheels within the main landing gear assembly. In Boeing parlance, the orientation is referred to as the 'truck positioner' (or truck tilt actuator), while in Airbus' terminology it's referred to as the 'bogie pitch trimmer.'.

The toe-down position is one of the easiest ways to visually identify a landing Boeing 767 from other Boeing widebodies, although not so much from Airbus aircraft, as some models have a similar configuration. Both Boeing and Airbus have switched the origination of the main landing gear within aircraft families depending on the requirements of the variant. Here is what to know about why Boeing designed the 767 (mostly) with toe-down landing gear and how that fits in with the wider industry.

In a recent development, the Boeing 767 has an unusual feature noted in the aviation community. It was designed with a conventional tricycle landing gear layout with a steerable twin-wheel nose gear and two four-wheel main landing gear bogies. When the 767 is airborne, its main landing gear bogies tilt forward in a toe-down position rather than the more conventional backward (toe-up) position. This is unique among Boeing aircraft.

It has been revealed that the Boeing 767 comes in several variants: the 767-200, the 767-2C (KC-46A), the 767-200ER, the 767-300, the 767-300ER, the 767-300F, and the 767-400ER. Boeing developed the 767-400ER in the 1990s as a stretched aircraft for a limited lineup of airlines. The -400ER was the first Boeing widebody aircraft that resulted from two fuselage stretches.

The variant was ultimately unpopular, with only 37 examples being ordered by the two US-based airlines (Delta Air Lines and Continental), plus one testbed eventually delivered to Bahrain as a VIP transport. Boeing likely lost money on the program, although it never published the financial figures for it. The notable feature of the variant for this article is that Boeing replaced the standard 767 landing gear with taller, heavier 777-derived landing gear. This required a redesigned structure and deeper fairing. Consequently, the -400ER is the only 767 variant with standard backward tilting landing gear.

In a recent development, the 767 has a narrower cross-section than other widebodies like the 747 or Airbus A300, being designed as a mid-sized airplane for seven-abreast seating (2-3-2). The novel design is often credited with solving multiple issues. One benefit often seen mentioned by pilots and mechanics on aviation forums is that the configuration allows the gear to fit into a smaller wheel well. Some describe it as a "tight fit" and the best use of limited space.

According to recent reports, the design avoids the need for large, drag-inducing blisters on the aircraft's belly. Another benefit was the Tilt Actuator Mechanism and how the aircraft lands. The tilt changes the aircraft's touchdown. The front wheels of each bogie make contact with the runway first, with the bogie then rotating level and the rear wheels settling. Some commentators say this helps to cushion the landing by spreading out the load more gradually and reducing stress on the landing gear.

Toe-up main landing gear (aft/rear wheels lower).

747 (wing gear only), 767-400ER (777-derived gear), 777, 777X, 787.

In a recent development, the design comes with a de-rotation tendency, naturally pitching the nose slightly downward toward the runway on contact. This requires pilots to hold back pressure carefully during the flare in order to avoid a firm nose-gear slap. The advantages of the toe-up design were not enough for Boeing to retain it with other aircraft. It has not used the design for subsequent aircraft like the Boeing 777, 767-400ER, and 787.

The classic Boeing widebody is still going strong.

Almost all narrowbody airliners come with a single set of main landing gear wheels. Here, the Boeing 757 stands out due to being a large narrowbody designed to fill the mid-sized airplane gap. It is often categorized as a heavy narrowbody, sitting at the upper weight limit of narrowbodies—up to 255,000 lbs (115.6 t) MTOW on later models. Boeing's aims to develop the replacement Upcoming Mid-Sized Airplane, often called the 797, have not materialized.

It has been revealed that the Boeing 757's bogies tilt slightly toe-down during flight. This means that the Boeing 767 is, strictly speaking, not unique among Boeing aircraft, but it remains more noticeable. The 757's bogies are slightly toe-down at around 5° to 8°, which is just enough to align the truck with the narrow fuselage wheel well during retraction. By comparison, the Boeing 767's angle is typically around 15°–17°.

It has been revealed that it can also be noted that the Boeing 757 is closely related to the Boeing 767 widebody. It is useful to think of the Boeing 757 and 767 as fraternal twins developed in the late 1970s. They were designed to allow aircraft to enjoy interchangeability and minimal pilot training between types. The 757 has long been a favored aircraft on thinner transatlantic routes, although it is now being replaced by the A321neo.

The Boeing 767 has been an excellent airliner, with Boeing selling around 1,380 examples. Over time, its comparatively robust and heavy design that has made it particularly useful as a freighter compared with modern composite material aircraft. However, this also gave it an economic disadvantage as a commercial passenger airliner, and Boeing replaced it with the cleansheet Boeing 787 Dreamliner. That composite-heavy aircraft offers around 25% better fuel efficiency.

According to recent reports, however, the Dreamliner did not replace the 767 as a freighter with the 787. Boeing continued to offer the 767, and companies continued to order it. In the end, it was stricter regulations that made the 767-300F infeasible as a freighter. The program is currently in the process of winding down (more below). The last of these freighters may continue flying into the 2050s or 2060s.

The passenger 767 fleet is approaching the end of its passenger career with airlines having phased out earlier models and leading operators (e.g., Delta, United, JAL, ANA) phasing them out and/or ordering their replacements. Delta withdrew three 767-300ERs in 2025 and another one so far in 2026, with the remaining -300ERs to be divested by 2030. Japan Airlines plans to retire and replace its fleet with the A321neo by 2028.

Dissecting the undercarriage of two revolutionary jetliners.

It has been revealed that as of November 2026, Boeing has delivered 13 767-300Fs, leaving it with a remaining backlog of seven aircraft. Deliveries of the Boeing 767-300F freighter are fast coming to an end, although deliveries of the military Boeing 767-2C (KC-46A Pegasus) tanker are set to continue deep into the 2030s. The FAA provided an exemption from new emission restrictions for the Boeing 767-300F until 2033 under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024.

The FAA only has jurisdiction in the United States, with the regulations in force elsewhere in the world. Consequently, Boeing sought to deliver all its outstanding orders for the Boeing 767 in 2026 ( regulations enter into force on January 1, 2027). Boeing's 2026 records show it delivered the two outstanding 767-300Fs to FedEx in April and May and 11 of the remaining orders to UPS between February and October.

Now, Boeing's records only show seven remaining to be delivered to an 'unidentified customer'. These remaining orders appear to be for UPS (considered an open secret), with Boeing starting the year with eight units for unidentified customers, and that number is now seven. That aircraft apparently went to UPS. The order was placed in December 2024 and is likely to be the last set of commercial 767s to be delivered.

Sources indicate that toe-down main landing gear is much more common on Airbus aircraft. Airbus models with toe-down landing gear include the Airbus A350-900, the Airbus A380, and the A310. With the A350-900, the four-wheel bogies tilt toe-down by around 9.3° in flight, allowing them to align cleanly with the ceiling of the center fuselage bay. This was flipped on the stretched A350-1000. The -1000 features a six-wheel bogie and has a slight toe-up bias.

Sources indicate that the A380 Superjumbo comes with a four-wheel wing gear bogie and six-wheel body gear bogies. Both of these bogies tilt down. The older A310 has a slight toe-down position on its main bogies, a departure from the mostly flat position on the earlier A300. Almost none of this conversation is relevant to the world's lineup of narrowbody aircraft, including the Boeing 737, Boeing 757, Airbus A320 family, A220, Embraer E-Jets, and Comac C919.

This is because these smaller aircraft use a single-axle, two-wheel main landing gear configuration. Put another way, there is nothing to tilt up or down. Exceptions are the Boeing 757 (mentioned above), some Tupolev airliners (e.g., Tu-154), a bizarre custom order of Indian Airlines A320s (1989 to early 1990s) with custom four-wheel main gear bogies, and early jetliners. All the early jetliners were retired as scheduled passenger aircraft.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that virgin Atlantic, like many other airlines, has been making several changes to its route network this year. Since March, the airline has completely withdrawn from the Middle East, and it recently confirmed that it will not resume flights between Manchester Airport (MAN) and Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) for summer 2027.

The decision comes as the SkyTeam member is basing a fifth aircraft at its Manchester hub next summer. It has also confirmed intends to increase frequencies on several existing routes as part of its summer 2027 schedule.

Since tensions in the Middle East escalated in late February, several airlines have temporarily paused or cut flights to the region. Virgin Atlantic was no exception. Before its withdrawal, the airline served two destinations in the region: Dubai International Airport (DXB) in the United Arab Emirates and King Khalid International Airport (RUH) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The latter was a relatively new addition to its network, having rolled out in March 2025.

The airline operated daily seasonal flights between London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and Dubai using its Airbus A350-1000 aircraft. Its Riyadh service, on the other hand, operated daily throughout the year using the Airbus A350-900. Initially, the UK airline announced that it was temporarily suspending both routes due to escalating tensions in the region. However, it subsequently decided to cancel them permanently.

Recent findings suggest that according to data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, Virgin Atlantic's last scheduled flights to both destinations were in mid-March 2026, and no further services are right now scheduled. Separately, its London Heathrow–Tel Aviv route (which it last operated in 2023 when the conflict began) remains suspended, and flights are not expected to resume.

Industry observers note that furthermore, another notable change came recently when Virgin Atlantic confirmed that it would not return to Las Vegas from the Northwest England airport next summer. The airline first launched flights between the two cities in 2011 and continued operating the route until 2019. It then reinstated services in June 2024.

Sources indicate that this year, the SkyTeam member operated the route between April and October and was scheduled to return on April 13, 2027, running through October 31. The airline had planned three weekly services, reducing to two during the peak summer months. However, these flights have now been canceled. Well, the route's performance may help explain the decision.

It has been revealed that according to data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT), Virgin Atlantic filled just 72.3% of its seats between Manchester and Las Vegas in the 12 months to July 2026. This was around ten percentage points lower than its London Heathrow–Las Vegas route, where it operates daily year-round flights using a 258-seat Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner.

Instead of daily flights to Dubai, the airline will increase its capacity to South Africa, adding a new destination and increasing frequency.

The Las Vegas cancelation comes as Virgin Atlantic has unveiled intends to increase frequencies on its three remaining US routes from the airport. According to the airline's original schedule for July 2027, it had planned 24 weekly departures across these three routes. That number will now increase to 40.

Sources indicate that flights to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) will increase from daily to 11 weekly, while services to Upcoming York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) will rise from seven to up to ten weekly. Orlando International Airport (MCO) will see the largest increase, from 12 to up to 19 weekly flights.

That noted, London Heathrow will continue to account for the majority of Virgin Atlantic's transatlantic capacity, representing roughly 84% of its transatlantic flying. The airline will continue to offer regular flights to 11 US destinations from the West London airport, including JFK, Boston, Atlanta, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Miami, Orlando, Seattle, Tampa and Washington, DC.
